set.statement: In three placebo-controlled trials in people with methamphetamine dependence or moderate to severe methamphetamine use disorder, mirtazapine was followed by somewhat less methamphetamine use than placebo on each trial's primary measure, although most participants kept using. Two trials from one San Francisco team, in men who have sex with men without current major depression (mean baseline CES-D depression scores about 17 and 20) with methamphetamine dependence who all received weekly counselling (60 men treated for 12 weeks; 120 cisgender men and transgender women treated for 24 weeks and followed 12 weeks after stopping), found a lower modelled weekly probability of a methamphetamine-positive urine: relative risk 0.57 (95% CI 0.35–0.93) at 12 weeks in the first trial and 0.67 (0.51–0.87) at 12 weeks in the second, with net relative risks of 0.75 (0.56–1.00) at 24 weeks and 0.73 (0.57–0.96) 12 weeks after medication stopped. Most urine samples stayed positive in both arms (66% vs 78% of samples provided at week 12 of the second trial), end-of-treatment abstinence did not differ significantly (18% vs 8%; OR 2.50, 0.80–7.61), adherence measured by electronic pill containers was below 50% in both arms, and drowsiness was more common on mirtazapine. These two trials share investigators, site, population and analysis model, so they are not independent replications of each other. A larger trial from a different team, one of whose authors is also an author of the first trial (344 adults randomized and 339 treated at six Australian public clinics; 37% women and 49% with a PHQ-9 depression score of 10 or more; given referral information and free to use other services, with no trial counselling described; treated for 12 weeks), found 2.2 fewer self-reported days of use in the past 28 days at week 12 than with placebo (95% CI 0.2–4.2; rate ratio 0.89, 0.80–0.98), from baseline means of 23.1 and 22.0 days, leaving both arms using on about 16 to 17 of 28 days (editors' calculation). It found no difference in methamphetamine-negative oral-fluid tests (13.2% vs 12.0% of samples; difference 1.3 points, −4.7 to 7.2) or in depression, sleep, HIV risk behaviour or quality of life; drowsiness (47% vs 33%) and weight gain (10% vs 3%) were more common on mirtazapine, 23% vs 15% stopped the medication for reasons related to it, and no outcome after the 12 weeks of treatment is reported. These trials treated methamphetamine dependence over months; the short trials of mirtazapine for the withdrawal period itself, reported in the claim on medicines for withdrawal, are different trials: pooled, they showed no difference from placebo in discontinuation, and one of them reported lower withdrawal scores, a result the review could not pool.
set.plain: Three trials have compared the antidepressant mirtazapine with a placebo in people with meth dependence. Two small trials by one San Francisco team, in gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (and a few transgender women) who also had weekly counselling, found that mirtazapine may lower the chance of a meth-positive urine test by roughly a quarter to two-fifths. In the larger of those two trials, the share of people who stopped using did not clearly differ between the groups. A larger trial by a different team (one of its researchers also worked on the first San Francisco trial), at six clinics in Australia, also included women and people with symptoms of depression. People given mirtazapine reported using meth on about 2 fewer days in 4 weeks than people given placebo, but both groups still used on most days, and saliva drug tests showed no difference. In all three trials most people kept using and drowsiness was more common on mirtazapine; in the Australian trial weight gain was too, and more people stopped taking it. Two other, short trials of mirtazapine for withdrawal symptoms are a separate question, described elsewhere in this section.
set.population: People with DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence (two San Francisco trials: cisgender men and transgender women who have sex with men, without current major depression, with a methamphetamine-positive urine at entry, receiving weekly counselling) or DSM-5 moderate to severe methamphetamine use disorder (one trial of adults at six Australian public outpatient clinics, using at least twice a week, with a positive amphetamine screen, not taking prescribed antidepressants)
set.exposure: Mirtazapine daily for 12 weeks (first San Francisco trial and the Australian trial) or 24 weeks (second San Francisco trial)
set.comparator: Matched placebo, with the same weekly counselling in the San Francisco trials and the same referral information and access to other services in the Australian trial
set.outcome: Methamphetamine-positive weekly urine (qualitative test) and end-of-treatment urine-defined abstinence (San Francisco trials); self-reported days of methamphetamine use in the past 28 days and methamphetamine-negative oral fluid (Australian trial)
set.magnitude: First trial (n=60): RR 0.57 (0.35–0.93) at 12 weeks; raw final-visit positivity 44% vs 63% (editors' RR 0.71, 0.42–1.18). Second trial (n=120): RR 0.67 (0.51–0.87) at 12 weeks; net RR 0.75 (0.56–1.00) at 24 weeks and 0.73 (0.57–0.96) at 36 weeks; raw positivity 66% vs 78%, 63% vs 74% and 71% vs 88%; end-of-treatment abstinence 18% vs 8% (OR 2.50, 0.80–7.61). Editors' crude week-12 risk ratio in the second trial, from the samples provided (25 of 38 vs 32 of 41): 0.84 (0.64–1.12). The modelled risk ratios measure how far the two arms' fitted trends diverged after allowing for the fitted baseline difference; the mirtazapine arm began with more positive urines (85% vs 75%), one reason the modelled ratios lie further from 1 than the crude contrasts (editors' reading). Australian trial (344 randomized, 339 analysed): days of use in the past 28 days fell by 7.0 vs 4.8 from baseline means of 23.1 vs 22.0; difference −2.2 days (−4.2 to −0.2), rate ratio 0.89 (0.80–0.98) at week 12; −1.3 (−3.3 to 0.6) at week 4 and −1.9 (−3.9 to 0.1) at week 8; editors' estimate of days used at week 12, about 16.1 vs 17.2. Methamphetamine-negative oral fluid 13.2% vs 12.0% (difference 1.3 points, −4.7 to 7.2). Drowsiness 47% vs 33% and weight gain 10% vs 3% (editors' risk differences 13.6, 3.3 to 23.9, and 6.9, 1.7 to 12.0 percentage points); medication stopped for reasons related to it 23% vs 15%.
set.grade.reasoning: Three double-blind placebo-controlled trials (519 participants analysed: 60, 120 and 339). Risk of bias, one level: in the first trial the registered primary outcome was changed from feasibility to efficacy during recruitment; in the second, 34–41% of urine results were missing at each assessment, with more dropout on mirtazapine, and the analysis assumes data missing completely at random; in the third, the only significant result is on self-reported use, drowsiness (47% vs 33%) could have revealed allocation, no blinding check is reported and the article does not describe allocation concealment. Inconsistency, one level: on drug tests the two San Francisco trials found lower modelled urine positivity, while the larger Australian trial found no difference in negative oral-fluid samples (13.2% vs 12.0%), and its effect on self-reported use (rate ratio 0.89) is smaller than the San Francisco estimates (0.57 to 0.75); population, counselling, outcome and type of test may explain part of this, but no analysis shows it. This between-trial difference is a separate problem from the third trial's reliance on self-report, which is counted under risk of bias. Indirectness no longer rated down: the Australian trial adds women, people with depressive symptoms and public clinics without trial counselling, and the outcomes are measures of use; people taking antidepressants, pregnant people and people with a recent suicide attempt remain excluded. Imprecision considered but not rated down: each trial's primary interval excludes no effect, although the Australian interval reaches a trivial 0.2 days and the second trial's 24-week interval reaches 1.00. Status replicated (METHODS §6.4): the Australian trial comes from a different team, sponsor, country, population and analysis model and agrees in direction on its primary outcome; one of its authors (Steven Shoptaw, listed for concept and design) is also an author of the first San Francisco trial (author lists of both papers), which the senior author may judge enough to keep the label replicated by the same team. The second San Francisco trial reports that its effect stayed significant when missing urine samples were counted as positive, when week-1 results were included and when baseline correlates of missingness were adjusted for, with the estimates only in a supplement the editors have not read; the analysis stratified by intensity of use showed no significant effect, and a blinding check at week 24 found 46% vs 49% guessing their arm correctly (P = .83). The Australian trial's primary estimate is reported as robust to multiple imputation and to adjustment for baseline covariates (supplement not read).

so they are not five independent replications. A later meta-analysis of bupropion (Bakouni et al., 2023; searched to October 2022) pooled a different outcome, the share of amphetamine-positive urine samples, from seven reports of six trials: risk ratio 0.90 (95% CI 0.84–0.96; very low certainty by the review's own rating); for bupropion alone (five trials, 357 participants) 0.90 (0.81–1.00), the rest coming from the two stages of a trial that combined bupropion with injectable naltrexone. That analysis counts each of 15,664 urine samples as an independent observation, so its intervals are too narrow; it reports no absolute rates, the largest bupropion-alone trial gave it no urine data, and retention did not differ (risk ratio 0.97, 0.89–1.05).

so a modest benefit or harm cannot be ruled out. A later review of bupropion trials found about one-tenth fewer meth-positive urine tests than with placebo, but this is uncertain: it treated every test as if it came from a different person, part of the data came from a trial that also gave a second medicine (naltrexone), and for bupropion on its own the result could also mean no effect.

set.population: People with methamphetamine dependence in placebo-controlled trials (five trials for abstinence; 14 trials of amphetamine or methamphetamine use disorder for retention); eight placebo-controlled trials of bupropion in amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder (later meta-analysis of the share of positive urine samples)
set.exposure: Bupropion or modafinil (abstinence); bupropion, modafinil, methylphenidate or dexamphetamine (retention); bupropion alone or with injectable naltrexone (share of positive urine samples)
set.outcome: Urine-verified abstinence in the last 2 weeks of treatment; retention to the end of the trial; share of amphetamine-positive urine samples (bupropion meta-analysis)
set.magnitude: Abstinence 19.8% vs 21.5%, OR 0.97 (0.65–1.45), I² 2%; 5 fewer per 1,000 (64 fewer to 69 more). Retention 53.0% vs 48.0%, OR 1.20 (0.91–1.58), I² 15%; 46 more per 1,000 (23 fewer to 113 more) against an assumed placebo retention of 480 per 1,000. Bakouni et al. (2023): share of amphetamine-positive urine samples, 7 reports, 15,664 samples, RR 0.90 (0.84–0.96), I² 89%; bupropion alone (5 trials, 357 participants) 0.90 (0.81–1.00); the two stages of the naltrexone-plus-bupropion trial 0.92 (0.89–0.94); intervals too narrow because samples, not people, are the unit of analysis; no event rates reported. Retention RR 0.97 (0.89–1.05), 7 reports, 786 participants.
set.grade.reasoning: Randomized trials. Risk of bias: allocation concealment inadequately reported in more than three-quarters of trials, outcome assessment unclear or high risk in all, incomplete outcome data at high risk in half. Imprecision, two levels: the interval runs from about a third fewer to nearly half again as many abstinent people, so neither a useful benefit nor a harm is excluded, and only 132 people were abstinent. The review's own downgrade for inconsistency is not applied (I² 2% and 15%). Nor are its indirectness downgrades (serious for abstinence, for pooling different drugs and doses; very serious for retention, which also pooled populations that included people who inject drugs, incarcerated people and people with ADHD): the claim is worded to the pooled drugs, doses and populations and speaks for no single drug or dose, and the test between the two drugs for abstinence was not significant (p = 0.59). The five abstinence trials come from two investigator groups, so 'replicated' rests on two groups, not on five independent trials (METHODS §6.3). Very low certainty means the result cannot be read as showing that these drugs do not work. The later bupropion meta-analysis (Bakouni et al., 2023) does not change the rating: its outcome (share of positive urine samples) differs from this claim's abstinence outcome; its intervals are too narrow because samples rather than people are the unit of analysis; its bupropion-alone estimate reaches no effect (0.90, 0.81–1.00); much of its estimate comes from a combination trial covered by the claim on naltrexone plus bupropion; it shares two of this claim's three bupropion trials (Shoptaw et al., 2008; Heinzerling et al., 2014), while the third (Anderson et al., 2015) gave it no urine data; and it rated its own urine result very low.
